nodes.text: AI agents increasingly need to act on the world through software (writing code, running it, browsing the web), but building and fairly evaluating such agents has generally meant assembling separate, often single-purpose infrastructure per project.
nodes.audience_note: Readers need 'agent' defined as an LLM-driven perceive-act loop over an environment, not a classifier.

nodes.text: Software agents are already being asked to fix GitHub issues, browse the web, and answer graduate-level questions; a shared, reusable, safely sandboxed platform lowers the cost of building and fairly comparing such agents, and this one is already widely used (MIT-licensed; 32K GitHub stars; 2.1K+ community contributions from 188+ contributors).

Existing open agent frameworks (AutoGPT, LangChain/LangGraph, MetaGPT, AutoGen, and others) each provide some mix of an interaction interface, an execution environment, and human/agent communication support.

These pieces tend to be provided individually and at varying depth -- for example, execution capability without a persistent, stateful session -- and dedicated software-engineering agents optimize a carefully designed interface for one task category rather than for breadth across categories.

Can one open platform, and one generalist agent built on it with a single fixed prompt, remain competitive across software engineering, web browsing, and miscellaneous reasoning/tool-use tasks at once?
Build such a platform and evaluate one generalist agent implementation on it across an integrated, broad benchmark suite spanning all three categories, with no per-benchmark prompt engineering.

An event-stream architecture connects users, agents, and the environment; a Docker-sandboxed runtime exposes bash, an IPython server, and a Playwright browser; an AgentSkills library forms an extensible agent-computer interface; agents may delegate subtasks to one another.
CodeAct: the agent's action is executable code (Python/bash) or a browser command, rather than a fixed menu of JSON tool calls.

Agent-Computer Interface (ACI): the set of tools and affordances exposed to an agent beyond raw code execution; SWE-Agent's own contribution was showing that a carefully designed ACI matters for solving complex tasks.
Evaluate the unmodified generalist agent on seven software-engineering benchmarks (SWE-Bench Lite, HumanEvalFix, BIRD, ML-Bench, BioCoder, Gorilla APIBench, ToolQA) against reproducible baselines.

On SWE-Bench Lite the agent resolves 26.0% of issues, within the spread of specialized open SWE baselines (18.0-27.3%); on HumanEvalFix it fixes 79.3% of bugs 0-shot, above all non-agentic baselines but below a 1-shot SWE-Agent baseline; on the remaining five software benchmarks its best configuration exceeds the non-agentic baselines shown, and on ToolQA one configuration badly underperforms while another leads the table.
Evaluate a browsing-specialized agent, and the generalist agent delegating to it, on WebArena and MiniWoB++ against specialized/trained web-agent baselines.

On WebArena the best OpenHands configuration reaches 15.5%, below two of the four specialized baselines shown; on MiniWoB++ its best result (40.8%) trails a specialist reinforcement-learning baseline (91.1%) by a wide margin.

Evaluate the generalist agent (via GPTSwarm for GAIA) on six miscellaneous reasoning/tool-use benchmarks (GAIA, GPQA, AgentBench, MINT-math, MINT-code, ProofWriter, Entity Deduction Arena) against task-specific baselines.
The agent exceeds its comparison baseline on GAIA, GPQA-diamond, AgentBench, MINT-math, and ProofWriter, and falls below it on MINT-code and Entity Deduction Arena.

Because the identical, unmodified agent and prompt is the one scored in every table, and no comparison baseline appears in more than one category's table, this mostly-competitive, occasionally-below-baseline pattern across all three categories at once is evidence for the platform's stated design goal of generality, not merely for strength on any single benchmark.

A single open platform -- event stream, sandboxed action space, ACI tool library, multi-agent delegation, and a 15-benchmark evaluation harness -- on which one generalist, fixed-prompt agent achieves broad cross-category competitiveness, closing the gap left by frameworks that provide this infrastructure only piecemeal.
No repeated-run variance is reported for any success-rate number across the 15 benchmarks.
Cross-agent comparisons vary the backbone LLM rather than holding it fixed against baselines, confounding platform design with model capability.
OpenHands is not the top performer on several individual benchmarks (WebArena, MiniWoB++, HumanEvalFix vs. a 1-shot baseline, MINT-code, Entity Deduction Arena, and one ToolQA configuration).
Benchmark subsets, hint-text exclusion, and baseline provenance (drawn from cited papers rather than re-run under identical conditions) vary across rows in ways that limit direct comparability.

The evaluated architecture (versions v1.5-v1.8) is a specific snapshot; later project material describes a substantially restructured system (a separate SDK, a 'V1' runtime, and an 'Agent Canvas' front end).
No experiment isolates which platform component (event stream, sandbox, ACI library, delegation) is responsible for the cross-category result.

If confirmed with controlled comparisons, this suggests that unifying agent infrastructure around one general action space can substitute for per-domain agent specialization, which bears on how future agent platforms allocate engineering effort.

The authors identify concrete next steps: richer multi-modality, stronger agents via training and inference-time techniques, better long-file editing, browsing improvements (integrating a Reflexion-based retry strategy), and automatic workflow generation.

experiment_chains.experiment: Software-engineering benchmark suite (SWE-Bench Lite, HumanEvalFix, BIRD, ML-Bench, BioCoder, Gorilla APIBench, ToolQA)
experiment_chains.hypothesis: The generalist agent, unmodified, resolves real software-engineering tasks at a rate comparable to agents built specifically for this category.
experiment_chains.falsifier: The generalist agent trails every specialized SWE baseline by a wide margin on most of the seven benchmarks.
experiment_chains.design_rationale: Software engineering is the category the platform's action space (sandboxed code execution, AgentSkills file editing) was most directly built for, making it the most direct first test of whether generality costs specialization.
experiment_chains.next: Software tasks alone cannot show generality across different interaction modalities; the next test moves to web browsing, exercising the browser action space instead of the code-execution path.

experiment_chains.hypothesis: The same platform, instantiated as a browsing-specialized agent (and via delegation from the generalist agent), completes realistic and synthetic web tasks competitively.
experiment_chains.falsifier: OpenHands' web agents fall far below every specialized/trained web-agent baseline on both benchmarks.
experiment_chains.design_rationale: WebArena tests realistic, free-form browsing; MiniWoB++ tests short, synthetic, reward-defined tasks; together they separate open-ended planning from low-level control while both stressing the browser action primitives rather than the code-execution path.
experiment_chains.next: Web results alone leave open whether competitiveness holds outside software/web interfaces entirely; the final test moves to heterogeneous reasoning and tool-use tasks with no shared interface at all.

experiment_chains.experiment: Miscellaneous reasoning/tool-use benchmark suite (GAIA, GPQA, AgentBench, MINT, ProofWriter, Entity Deduction Arena)
experiment_chains.hypothesis: The same underlying agent design, with no category-specific redesign, remains competitive on tasks that are neither software engineering nor web browsing.
experiment_chains.falsifier: OpenHands trails its comparison baseline on most of these six benchmarks.
experiment_chains.design_rationale: This category shares the least with the platform's original code/browser action space, making it the strongest available test of whether the platform's generality is genuine rather than an artifact of the first two, more code/browser-centric, categories.
experiment_chains.next: With all three categories tested on the identical agent design, the paper synthesizes the cross-category pattern into its central, structurally-grounded generality claim (C016).
